questions.question: A team wants to self-host Llama on their own GPUs with an optimized inference engine and an OpenAI-compatible API, without building the serving stack themselves. Which NVIDIA offering fits best?
options: NVIDIA cuDF
NVIDIA Nsight Systems
NVIDIA NIM microservices
NeMo Curator
questions.explanation: NIM packages models as prebuilt, GPU-optimized inference containers that expose industry-standard (OpenAI-compatible) APIs and run on your own infrastructure or in the cloud. cuDF is dataframes, Curator is data curation and Nsight is profiling.

questions.question: An app already uses the OpenAI Python client. What is usually needed to point it at an NVIDIA NIM endpoint instead?
options: Retrain the model on the NIM server
Change the base URL, API key and model name
Rewrite the app in C++ against the TensorRT API
Convert all prompts into ONNX format
questions.explanation: NIM for LLMs exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as /v1/chat/completions, so existing clients work by changing the base_url, the key and the model identifier. No retraining or model conversion is needed in the app.

questions.question: When a NIM container for an LLM starts on a given GPU, how does it get good performance without manual tuning?
options: It picks an optimized engine profile for the detected GPU
It runs requests on the CPU and caches the results on the GPU
It converts the weights to FP64 for maximum numerical accuracy
It fine-tunes the model on the GPU during its first startup
questions.explanation: NIM includes optimized inference backends and picks a profile matching the detected GPU type, count and precision. Optimized engines such as TensorRT-LLM are used where available, with other backends as fallback.

questions.question: A company serves a PyTorch model, an ONNX model and a TensorRT engine and wants one serving platform for all three. What fits best?
options: cuML, with a scikit-learn wrapper around each model
NeMo Curator, with a GPU data pipeline per model
Triton Inference Server, with a backend per framework
NeMo Guardrails, with a rail per model framework
questions.explanation: Triton is open-source inference serving software with backends for TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and more. It serves them side by side with shared features such as batching and metrics.

questions.question: Many small, independent requests reach a Triton-served model and GPU utilization is low. Which feature combines them on the server to raise throughput?
options: Response caching
Dynamic batching
The sequence batcher's state
Model versioning
questions.explanation: Triton's dynamic batcher combines individual inference requests into larger batches on the server, which uses the GPU far more efficiently. max_queue_delay_microseconds controls how long it may wait to form a batch.

questions.question: In Triton's dynamic batcher, what is the effect of increasing max_queue_delay_microseconds?
options: Larger batches can form: more throughput, more latency
Each batch is split across more GPU instances
The model loads faster when the server starts up
Requests skip the queue: lower latency, less throughput
questions.explanation: The queue delay is how long the scheduler may hold requests to build a bigger batch. More delay can improve throughput but adds latency, so it is a trade-off to tune, for example with Model Analyzer.

questions.question: A Triton model has one instance per GPU and requests queue up while the GPU still has headroom. Which configuration lets several copies of the model execute concurrently?
options: Add more version folders to the model repository
Increase the count in instance_group
Disable metrics on port 8002
Set max_batch_size to 0
questions.explanation: By default Triton creates one execution instance per GPU. instance_group sets how many instances run in parallel (on GPU or CPU), which allows concurrent execution and better utilization. max_batch_size 0 disables batching.

source.title: Triton User Guide, Concurrent Model Execution

questions.question: A pipeline needs preprocessing, then a model, then postprocessing, chained inside Triton with no client round-trips between steps. Which Triton feature is designed for a fixed pipeline like this?
options: An ensemble model
A rate limiter
The sequence batcher
Model warmup
questions.explanation: Ensemble models define a DAG of steps in config.pbtxt, mapping the outputs of one model to the inputs of the next, so the whole pipeline runs server-side. For pipelines with loops or conditions, Business Logic Scripting (BLS) in the Python backend is used.

questions.question: A Triton pipeline must call different models depending on the input (if/else, loops). Which feature supports this custom control flow?
options: More instances in the model's instance_group, one per branch
Business Logic Scripting (BLS) in the Python backend
A static ensemble defined in config.pbtxt
The dynamic batcher with priority levels
questions.explanation: Ensembles are static graphs. BLS lets Python backend code call other models from its execute function, so it can implement conditionals and loops.

source.title: Triton User Guide, Business Logic Scripting

questions.question: What is the required layout of a Triton model repository?
options: One Python file per model, with versions tracked by git tags
A single archive file holding every model and one shared config file
A folder per model with config.pbtxt and numbered version subfolders
A SQL table with one row and one binary blob per model
questions.explanation: Each model directory has at least one numeric version subdirectory, such as 1/model.onnx, and usually a config.pbtxt. Triton loads models from this repository, which can also live on S3, GCS or Azure.

questions.question: An operator wants to scrape Triton's GPU utilization, request counts and queue times into Grafana. Where does Triton expose these by default?
options: Only in the server's stdout logs, as plain text lines
A Prometheus endpoint, by default at port 8002 /metrics
In each model's config.pbtxt, updated every minute
Through the gRPC inference port 8001, on request only
questions.explanation: Triton publishes Prometheus metrics, such as nv_inference_request_success, nv_inference_queue_duration_us and GPU metrics collected via DCGM, at http://localhost:8002/metrics by default. HTTP inference is on 8000 and gRPC on 8001.

questions.question: A team needs to measure throughput and latency of a model on Triton and then find the best batch size and instance count. Which two NVIDIA tools are designed for this? (Select two.)
options: cuDF
NeMo Curator
Triton Model Analyzer
perf_analyzer
NeMo Guardrails
questions.explanation: perf_analyzer generates load (by concurrency or request rate) and reports throughput and latency. Model Analyzer sweeps configurations such as max batch size, dynamic batching and instance groups to find an optimal configuration under constraints.

questions.question: A stateful model must receive all requests of one sequence (e.g. a streaming audio session) on the same model instance, in order. Which Triton scheduler is required?
options: No scheduler: Triton does not support stateful models
The ensemble scheduler
The sequence batcher
The dynamic batcher
questions.explanation: Stateful models need correlated requests routed to the same instance. Triton's sequence batcher does this using sequence IDs and start/end flags. The dynamic batcher is for stateless models.

source.title: Triton User Guide, Concurrent Model Execution (stateful models)

questions.question: What is NVIDIA TensorRT?
options: A vector database for storing and searching model embeddings
A framework for training large models from scratch on multi-GPU clusters
A data-labeling tool that prepares training sets for GPUs
An SDK that compiles trained models into optimized GPU inference engines
questions.explanation: TensorRT takes trained models, typically via ONNX or PyTorch, and builds engines optimized for a target GPU: it chooses the fastest kernels, fuses layers and uses reduced precisions such as FP16, FP8 or INT8. It is for inference, not training.

questions.question: Which two optimizations does TensorRT apply when building an engine? (Select two.)
options: Fusing layers and tensors to reduce kernel launches and memory traffic
Adding extra layers to the network to increase its accuracy
Converting the model so that it runs only on the CPU, not the GPU
Re-training the model on new data to adapt it to the target GPU
Selecting the fastest kernels for the target GPU (kernel auto-tuning)
questions.explanation: TensorRT's builder fuses compatible operations, picks the fastest implementation of each layer for the specific GPU, and can lower precision. It doesn't change the architecture's capacity or retrain the model.

questions.question: An engineer builds a TensorRT engine on an A100 and copies the engine file to a server with a different GPU architecture. What should they expect?
options: It may fail or be suboptimal; rebuild it for the target GPU
It runs identically on any NVIDIA GPU of any architecture
It falls back to running on the CPU at the same speed
It converts itself back to ONNX and rebuilds automatically
questions.explanation: TensorRT engines are optimized for, and by default tied to, the GPU architecture and TensorRT version they were built with. The portable artifact is the ONNX (or framework) model, which is rebuilt into an engine per target.

questions.question: Which two statements about exporting a PyTorch model to ONNX for deployment are correct? (Select two.)
options: TensorRT includes an ONNX parser to import such models
A GPU can only run models that are stored in ONNX format
ONNX is an open, framework-neutral format for describing models
ONNX encrypts the model weights by default to protect the IP
Exporting to ONNX makes the model train noticeably faster on GPUs
questions.explanation: ONNX defines standard operators and a file format (a graph serialized with Protocol Buffers), so models from different frameworks can be consumed by runtimes and compilers. TensorRT ships an ONNX parser for exactly this. ONNX doesn't affect training speed or encrypt weights.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Transitioning AI Models with ONNX

questions.question: A model exported to ONNX with torch.onnx.export (tracing) gives wrong results for inputs that take a different branch of an if-statement. Why?
options: ONNX cannot represent floating-point weights correctly
Tracing records only the path taken by the example input
The exporter randomizes branch order to save memory
ONNX graphs can contain only a single layer per model
questions.explanation: Tracing runs the model once with sample inputs and records that path, unrolling loops and fixing branches. Models with dynamic control flow need scripting or code that avoids data-dependent branches.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Transitioning AI Models with ONNX

questions.question: What is TensorRT-LLM?
options: A tokenizer library for multilingual LLM vocabularies
An open-source library for optimizing LLM inference on NVIDIA GPUs
A hosted chatbot product that runs only in NVIDIA's cloud
An open-source library for pre-training LLMs efficiently on CPU clusters
questions.explanation: TensorRT-LLM provides optimized kernels and runtime features for LLMs, such as in-flight batching, paged KV cache, quantization and speculative decoding. It integrates with Triton and is used inside NIM.

questions.question: With static batching, short requests wait until the longest request in the batch finishes. Which technique, supported by TensorRT-LLM, fixes this?
options: Larger static batches with padding
In-flight (continuous) batching
Beam search with more beams
A Triton model ensemble
questions.explanation: In-flight batching (also called continuous or iteration-level batching) evicts finished sequences and admits new requests at every generation step, which keeps the GPU busy and cuts waiting time.

source.title: TensorRT-LLM, Paged Attention, IFB and Request Scheduling

questions.question: What problem does a paged KV cache solve?
options: Wasted KV memory from reserving each request's maximum length
Inaccurate answers caused by a low sampling temperature
Having to rebuild the engine for every new GPU architecture
Slow tokenization of very long prompts before the prefill phase
questions.explanation: Paged KV caching (PagedAttention) stores each request's keys and values in fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous and are allocated on demand. Less memory is wasted, so more concurrent requests fit on the GPU.

source.title: TensorRT-LLM, Paged Attention, IFB and Request Scheduling

questions.question: Which of these NVIDIA GPU generations supports FP8 inference in TensorRT-LLM, thanks to FP8 Tensor Cores?
options: Kepler (e.g. K80)
Pascal (e.g. P100)
Volta (e.g. V100)
Hopper (e.g. H100)
questions.explanation: FP8 Tensor Cores arrived with Hopper (H100) and Ada Lovelace, and continue in Blackwell. TensorRT-LLM supports FP8 quantization on H100 and later. Pascal, Kepler and Volta have no FP8 Tensor Cores; Blackwell adds FP4.

questions.question: What is NVIDIA NeMo, in the broadest sense?
options: A GPU driver and CUDA runtime bundle for data-center servers and workstations
Libraries and microservices to build, customize, evaluate and guard GenAI
A vector database optimized for retrieval on NVIDIA GPUs
A single pretrained chatbot model released by NVIDIA
questions.explanation: NeMo covers the model lifecycle: training and post-training frameworks (Megatron-based), data curation (Curator), customization (Customizer), evaluation (Evaluator), retrieval (Retriever) and safety (Guardrails).

questions.question: A team must clean a multi-terabyte web-text corpus before pre-training: deduplicate it, filter low-quality text and identify languages, all on GPUs. Which NVIDIA tool is built for this?
options: NeMo Guardrails
Triton Inference Server
NeMo Curator
TensorRT
questions.explanation: NeMo Curator is a scalable, GPU-accelerated data curation library for text (and images, video, audio), with deduplication, quality filtering, language identification and classification. The others are for serving or safety.

questions.question: Which NeMo microservice is designed to fine-tune models on a company's proprietary data through an API?
options: NeMo Customizer
NeMo Guardrails
NeMo Curator
NeMo Retriever
questions.explanation: NeMo Customizer is the microservice for fine-tuning language models on your own data. Retriever provides embedding and reranking for RAG, Guardrails adds safety rails, and Curator prepares datasets.

questions.question: A team building an enterprise RAG pipeline wants NVIDIA's optimized embedding and reranking models as microservices. Which family provides them?
options: NeMo Curator
TensorRT Model Optimizer
cuGraph
NeMo Retriever
questions.explanation: NeMo Retriever provides retrieval building blocks for RAG, such as embedding and reranking NIMs, with privacy-preserving data access. Curator prepares training data, and cuGraph is graph analytics.

questions.question: Which NeMo component benchmarks models and agents with standard and custom metrics, including LLM-as-a-judge?
options: NeMo Evaluator
NeMo Customizer
NeMo Curator
NeMo Guardrails
questions.explanation: NeMo Evaluator is for benchmarking and monitoring model effectiveness, with academic benchmarks, custom metrics and LLM-as-a-judge. Customizer fine-tunes, Curator prepares data and Guardrails controls behaviour at runtime.

questions.question: Which NVIDIA library provides optimized collective communication such as all-reduce across multiple GPUs and nodes?
options: cuDF
TensorRT
cuDNN
NCCL
questions.explanation: NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) implements all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast and other collectives over NVLink, PCIe and InfiniBand. Distributed training uses it to synchronize gradients.

questions.question: Which NVIDIA library provides GPU-accelerated primitives for deep neural networks, such as convolutions, attention and normalization, used by frameworks like PyTorch?
options: cuDNN
cuGraph
DCGM
NCCL
questions.explanation: cuDNN is the CUDA Deep Neural Network library of tuned DL primitives that frameworks call under the hood. NCCL handles communication, cuGraph handles graphs and DCGM handles GPU monitoring.

questions.question: What are Tensor Cores?
options: A Python package for creating and manipulating tensors
General-purpose CPU cores added to GPU boards for data loading
A cloud service that stores model tensors between separate training runs
GPU units that accelerate matrix multiply-accumulate in low precision
questions.explanation: Tensor Cores perform mixed-precision matrix math (FP16, BF16, TF32, FP8, INT8 and more, depending on the generation) much faster than regular CUDA cores. They are central to DL training and inference speed.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of NVLink in multi-GPU servers?
options: A software license manager for multi-GPU servers
A network protocol for linking GPUs over the internet
A high-bandwidth direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect
A model compression technique for multi-GPU inference
questions.explanation: NVLink connects GPUs directly with far higher bandwidth than PCIe, which speeds up tensor parallelism and gradient synchronization across GPUs. NVSwitch extends it to all-to-all connectivity.

questions.question: A team wants pre-built, GPU-optimized containers for PyTorch, Triton and NeMo, plus pretrained models, from NVIDIA. Where do they get them?
options: Matplotlib's gallery
The PyPI 'nvidia' package only
The CUDA driver installer
The NGC catalog
questions.explanation: NGC is NVIDIA's catalog of GPU-optimized containers, pretrained models, Helm charts and SDKs, including framework containers, Triton, NeMo and NIM images.

questions.question: An enterprise wants NVIDIA's AI software (NIM, Triton, NeMo, RAPIDS...) with enterprise support, security updates and API stability for production. What is that offering called?
options: CUDA Toolkit
NVIDIA AI Enterprise
NVIDIA GeForce Experience
NVIDIA Omniverse Create
questions.explanation: NVIDIA AI Enterprise is the supported software platform that includes NIM microservices, Triton, NeMo and other frameworks with enterprise support. Triton and NIM are both part of it.

questions.question: A team needs to find out why GPU utilization is low during training and check GPU health in a cluster. Which two NVIDIA tools fit? (Select two.)
options: DCGM, to monitor GPU health and telemetry across the cluster
The cuDF pandas accelerator, to speed up data loading
NeMo Guardrails, to block unsafe prompts during training
Nsight Systems, to profile the timeline of CPU and GPU activity
NeMo Curator, to deduplicate the training data on the GPU
questions.explanation: Nsight Systems shows a system-wide timeline (kernels, memory copies, CPU stalls) to find bottlenecks. DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) monitors and diagnoses GPUs at cluster scale, and Triton uses it for GPU metrics.

source.title: Triton User Guide, Metrics (GPU metrics via DCGM)

questions.question: What is CUDA?
options: A type of high-bandwidth memory used on data-center GPUs
A file format for exchanging trained models between frameworks
NVIDIA's platform and programming model for general GPU computing
A deep learning model architecture designed by NVIDIA research
questions.explanation: CUDA lets developers write GPU kernels in C/C++ (and via Python libraries) and is the foundation that cuDNN, NCCL, TensorRT, RAPIDS and the frameworks are built on.

questions.question: A developer wants to try NVIDIA-hosted models (e.g. Nemotron, Llama) through an API for prototyping, before deciding to self-host. Where is the quickest place to start?
options: The NVIDIA API catalog (build.nvidia.com) with hosted NIM endpoints
Compiling TensorRT-LLM from source and building engines locally
Downloading cuDNN and writing custom CUDA kernels for the model
Buying a DGX system and installing NVIDIA AI Enterprise first
questions.explanation: build.nvidia.com hosts NIM endpoints with OpenAI-compatible APIs for prototyping. The same NIM containers can later be self-hosted with NVIDIA AI Enterprise.
